title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion
summary: Two retrievers give you two ranked lists whose scores mean nothing to each other. RRF throws the scores away and adds up 1 over 60 plus rank. Tried on this course's own lessons: one query got better, one got worse, one stayed put, and the reason why is the lesson.
html:
Day 32 said keep a word index. Day 33 said you need it because embeddings cannot handle exact strings. So now you run both, and you have two ranked lists of results that you need to turn into one.

The obvious move is to add the scores up. You cannot, and it is worth seeing why clearly. From my own runs on this course's lessons, BM25 handed back a top score of 7.16 for one query and 3.91 for another. Cosine similarity on embeddings would have given something like 0.81 and 0.78 for the same two. The ranges are different, the spreads are different, and both change from query to query. Adding 7.16 to 0.81 is adding a temperature to a distance.

The trick: forget the scores, keep the positions

Reciprocal Rank Fusion ignores every score and looks only at where each document landed. A document at position r in a list contributes:

1 / (k + r)

r is the position in that list, 1 for the top hit.
k is a constant, almost always 60.

Add up a document's contributions across every list it appears in, then sort by the total. That is the whole algorithm. Ten lines of code, no training, no calibration, nothing to tune per query.

It works because position is the one thing that means the same in both systems. "Your best guess" is comparable across engines in a way that 7.16 and 0.81 are not.

Worked out on two lists of five

Say the word index returns A, B, C, D, E in that order, and the vector index returns F, A, C, B, D. With k set to 60:

DocWhere it placedRRF score
Awords #1, vectors #20.03252
Bwords #2, vectors #40.03175
Cwords #3, vectors #30.03175
Dwords #4, vectors #50.03101
Fvectors #1 only0.01639
Ewords #5 only0.01538

Look at F. It was the vector index's single best guess, its number one result, and it comes out fifth. Meanwhile D, which neither system rated higher than fourth, comes out above it.

That is not a bug. With k at 60, appearing in both lists roughly doubles your score, and the position within each list barely moves the needle: 1/61 and 1/65 differ by about four percent. So RRF at k = 60 is mostly counting how many systems liked you, with position as a tiebreaker. B and C come out separated by eight millionths, which tells you how little the exact positions matter here.

The behaviour that falls out is the one you usually want from a hybrid: two systems agreeing is stronger evidence than one system being very sure.

k is the only knob, and it means something

k decides how much you care about position versus agreement. Set it to 1 instead of 60 and the same two lists come out differently:

k = 60    A, B, C, D, F, E
k = 1     A, B, C and F tied, then D, E

F climbs from fifth to joint third, because at k = 1 being somebody's number one is worth 1/2 while being somebody's fourth is worth 1/5. Small k trusts confident single systems. Large k trusts consensus.

Everyone uses 60. It comes from the 2009 paper that introduced the method, where it was tuned on their test collections, and it has been copied ever since without much re-checking. Same situation as BM25's k1 = 1.2 from yesterday's lesson. It is a reasonable default, not a law, and if one of your two retrievers is clearly stronger than the other, k is not the right fix anyway. Weighted RRF is: multiply each list's contributions by a weight, 0.7 for the one you trust and 0.3 for the other.

If you want to see it measured

I do not have an embedding model in this container, so I could not do the real thing, words against vectors. Instead I fused two lexical systems over the 33 published lessons: one BM25 index over the full lesson text, one over just titles and summaries. Weaker demonstration, and the result is more interesting for it.

"why is my search returning the wrong answer for a product code"
   full text  -> day 32, BM25
   titles     -> day 1, What RAG actually is
   fused      -> day 33, identifiers          better

"how many bytes does one vector take"
   full text  -> day 15, Exact kNN            correct
   titles     -> day 21, Product quantization I
   fused      -> day 32, BM25                 worse

"overlap between chunks"
   full text  -> day 6, Chunking 101          correct
   titles     -> day 6, Chunking 101          correct
   fused      -> day 6, Chunking 101          same

One better, one worse, one unchanged. The middle row is the important one. The full text index had the right answer at position one, the title index was wrong, and fusing them lost the right answer. RRF has no idea that one of its inputs is weak. It is an average, and averaging something good with something bad gives you something in between.

So the rule is not "fusion improves things". It is that fusion helps when your systems fail in different places, and hurts when one is simply worse. Words and vectors are a good pair because their blind spots barely overlap. Two lexical indexes over the same text are a bad pair.

One accident worth noticing: yesterday the same query scored 3.98 and today it scored 3.91, because the corpus grew from 31 lessons to 33. Rarity weights are computed across the whole collection, so every score in a BM25 index shifts when you add documents. Nothing is wrong, but it does mean cached scores and thresholds go stale on every ingest.

If you remember one thing
RRF throws away incomparable scores and keeps comparable positions, adding 1/(60 + rank) across lists. It rewards agreement, and it only pays off when your retrievers fail in different places.

Tomorrow: SPLADE, which tries to get both behaviours out of one model by learning a sparse representation, so a document gets weights on words it does not actually contain.
exercise:
One. Write your day 34 note.

Two. Take the two lists from the worked example, words A B C D E and vectors F A C B D, and recompute the fusion with k = 5. Work out where F lands this time, given that it was fifth at k = 60 and joint third at k = 1. The answer is not halfway between the two, and seeing why is the point. Then say in one line what k you would pick if your word index was reliable and your vector index was experimental.
